title: Staged rollout: KV cache staleness and tokenizer-schema mismatch - incident review
summary: During a staged rollout of model variant v2.14 + tokenizer v3.1 to a 2% canary population, we observed systematic generation degradations and repetition in canary traffic. Root cause traced to a tokenizer schema change that altered cache key derivation combined with shared KV cache (Redis) namespace collisions between canary and prod, causing stale/incorrect KV cache reads. Immediate mitigation: disable KV caching for the new variant, flush affected cache namespace, and rollback canary. This doc captures timeline, technical root cause, mitigation steps taken, and recommended long-term fixes and runbook updates.
detection: Automated canary-quality monitors triggered at 2026-02-18T09:12:00Z: sudden spike in token-repetition score (+420%), increase in average perplexity on held-out prompt set (+26%), and a small but consistent rise in client error rate for chat-stream endpoints from 0.2% -> 0.9%. Pager alert routed to SRE on-call at 09:15 UTC. Noise in latency was minimal; the anomaly was quality-first (model output regressions) rather than classic 5xx availability.
timeline:
2026-02-18T08:50Z - Deploy started: runtime nodes for canary group (2% routing) received model v2.14 and tokenizer v3.1.
2026-02-18T09:10Z - Canary quality monitor alerted (token repetition + perplexity).
2026-02-18T09:15Z - Pager to SRE on-call (Aisha). Initial triage: suspect model weights.
2026-02-18T09:30Z - Run quick eval on canary nodes: short prompt set produced high repetition and mismatched token offsets.
2026-02-18T09:45Z - Checksum compare: tokenizer artifact checksum on canary nodes matched artifact, but cache key algorithm had changed (prefix bytes moved).
2026-02-18T10:05Z - Confirmed Redis keys being read by canary were produced earlier by prod nodes (namespace collision).
2026-02-18T10:25Z - Emergency mitigation: disable KV caching flag for v2.14, triggered cache-namespace flush for affected key prefix.
2026-02-18T10:40Z - Canary rollback initiated to v2.13 on canary nodes.
2026-02-18T11:05Z - Monitors stabilised; quality metrics returned near baseline.
2026-02-18T13:00Z - Post-incident coordination call; action items created.
impact: User-visible: minor increase in low-confidence hallucinations and repeated tokens for ~2% of routing traffic (canary population). No broad production user escalation. Internal: short-lived confidence drop in the canary experiment; blocked dependent rollout to 10% and full rollout. No data loss. Estimated exposed requests ~14k during 09:10-10:40 UTC window.
root_cause:
Multiple contributing factors combined: 
- Tokenizer v3.1 introduced a small change in serialized tokenizer metadata which altered the cache-key derivation (the 'tok-prefix' bytes moved within serialized header). This was not considered a cache schema change in the release checklist.
- The runtime relies on a shared Redis cluster without enforced tenant isolation for ephemeral canaries. Canary and prod share the same keyspace with a weak prefix scheme, so old prod keys could be read by canary nodes and vice versa.
- Deployment sequencing: tokenizer artifact deployed to canary before the rollout process validated cache-compatibility and before the cache garbage-collection job could run.
- Insufficient pre-rollout automated tests to simulate mixed-cache states (prod writes + canary reads).
immediate_mitigation:
Actions executed during incident: 
- Disabled KV caching for model variant v2.14 via runtime flag (runtime-config set caching.enabled=false for variant id).
- Flushed Redis keys matching 'kv:v2:*:tok-prefix' for affected namespace (careful TTL-aware flush to minimize blast radius).
- Rolled back canary routing to model v2.13 and pinned canary nodes to previous runtime image.
- Temporarily restricted canary-to-prod cache access by applying a read-only ACL rule on shared Redis to prevent further writes from mixing namespaces while we audited.
- Created JIRA-INC-7041 to track follow-ups.
rollback_decision: Rollback to v2.13 was chosen because disabling KV cache alone left risk of subtle state mismatch and because the canary's failure profile matched a cross-version cache-read problem. Rolling back restored a known-good model+tokenizer pair and the monitoring thresholds returned to baseline within ~25 minutes of rollback completion.
long_term_fix:
Planned and recommended fixes: 
- Enforce tenant-isolated cache namespaces for canary/reserved pools; no shared Redis keyspace between canary and production by default.
- Add an automated pre-rollout compatibility check that computes tokenizer checksum differences and runs a 'mixed-cache simulation' (write prods keys, read from canary) as part of the rollout pipeline.
- Expand rollout checklist to require explicit verification of cache key derivation when tokenizer or serialization changes are present.
- Improve runtime to support model-version-prefixed cache keys (schema v2) and a safe migration tool that can remap keys when deterministic changes are introduced.
- Add monitor for cache-miss spikes, mismatched token offset exceptions, and token-level perplexity deltas; escalate to pagers using a quality-first policy.
- Update runbook to include an immediate step to toggle caching flags and a safe pattern for namespace flushes (include sample commands and TTL-aware filters).

oncall_notes:
Useful commands and notes captured during oncall: 
- Inspect Redis key distribution: redis-cli --scan --pattern 'kv:v2:*:tok-prefix' | wc -l
- TTL-aware delete: redis-cli --scan --pattern 'kv:v2:*:tok-prefix' | xargs -n1 sh -c 'TTL=$(redis-cli ttl "${0}"); if [ "${TTL}" -gt 0 ]; then redis-cli del "${0}"; fi'
- Disable caching for variant: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SRE_API_KEY' https://runtime.internal/config/variants/v2.14 -d '{"caching.enabled":false}' (use API token scoped to staging)
- Rollback command (canary group): ./deploy/rollback --group canary --model v2.13 --force-restart
- Monitoring to watch post-mitigation: canary-quality/token-repetition, canary-quality/perplexity, endpoint-errors/chat-stream, redis-key-inserts/s1
- Note: when flushing keys, prefer prefix-limited and TTL-aware deletes. Full 'FLUSHALL' was considered dangerous and avoided.
- Slack shorthand used during incident: #ops-incidents thread EG5h2. Keep thread linked in ticket.
postmortem_notes:
Lessons learned: 
- Stateful caches are an anti-pattern for shared canary experiments unless isolation is enforced.
- Small serialization/tokenizer changes can have outsized impact because cache key derivation is brittle.
- The rollout pipeline needs better hooks for stateful component compatibility.
- Our monitoring suite was effective at catching a quality-first regression quickly; however, runbook steps to remediate these particular failures were missing.
- Cross-team coordination (infra-cache, serving-runtime, eng-sre, applied-ml) was good; ensure all stakeholders are looped into follow-up Jira tickets.

Immediate priorities: implement tenant isolation for caches and add the mixed-cache test in rollout CI. Schedule a follow-up review of the incident in the weekly SRE sync (agenda: review fixes, assign owners, confirm timelines).
